# Introduction

Most Kaggle Learn-style tabular projects — including this portfolio's
academic_success and CO2 Emissions projects — are supervised: there's a
`y` the model is trying to predict, and a metric that scores how close
its predictions come. **Recommendation** is a different kind of problem,
and it splits into two genuinely different techniques depending on what
data is available:

- **Content-based** — no user data needed at all. Compare items by their
  own measurable properties (here, Spotify's audio features) and
  recommend whatever's most similar.
- **Collaborative filtering** — no item content needed at all. Learn
  from real user/item interaction history (here, KKBox's listening
  logs) instead.

This report builds and evaluates one working system of each kind, then
puts them side by side — not because one technique "wins" in general
(they solve different problems, with different data requirements), but
because comparing how each is built, evaluated, and interpreted is a
more honest way to understand recommendation than presenting either one
in isolation.

# Part I — Content-Based Recommendation (Spotify)

Given a track someone likes, recommend other tracks whose *audio*
resembles it — not tracks other, similar listeners happened to play.
Every recommendation here comes from Spotify's own audio-feature
measurements: danceability, energy, acousticness, and so on. Built on
Kaggle's [Spotify Tracks
Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/maharshipandya/-spotify-tracks-dataset).

## Data

~114,000 tracks, roughly 1,000 sampled per genre across 114 genres, each
with:

- **Audio features** (Spotify's own per-track measurements):
  `danceability`, `energy`, `loudness`, `speechiness`, `acousticness`,
  `instrumentalness`, `liveness`, `valence` (musical positivity), `tempo`,
  `key` (one of 12 pitch classes), `mode` (major/minor), `time_signature`.
- **Metadata**: `track_name`, `artists`, `album_name`, `duration_ms`,
  `explicit`.
- **`popularity`** — a Spotify-computed score, and **`track_genre`** — a
  human-assigned genre tag. Neither is used as a recommender *input*
  feature (see Methodology) — both are reserved for evaluation.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based import config, data

tracks_df = data.load_tracks()
print(f"{len(tracks_df)} tracks, {tracks_df[config.GENRE_COL].nunique()} genres")
tracks_df[config.RAW_AUDIO_NUMERIC_COLS + [config.GENRE_COL, config.POPULARITY_COL]].describe(include="all").T
```

### Why `popularity` and `track_genre` are excluded from the feature space

Including `popularity` as a recommendation feature would make the system
chase what's already trending rather than what actually sounds similar —
the opposite of a useful recommender. Including `track_genre` directly
would make genre-matching in the evaluation below trivially easy (the
recommender would just be looking up the genre column), which would prove
nothing about whether the *audio* similarity is meaningful. Both are kept
out of the feature space and used only afterward, to score results.

## Feature engineering

Three engineered features, detailed in
`src/recommendation_showcase/content_based/features.py`:

- **`key_sin` / `key_cos`** — `key` is 12 pitch classes arranged in a
  circle (key 11 is one semitone from key 0, not "far away" from it), so
  it's encoded as a point on a circle rather than a plain integer or a
  flat one-hot encoding — the same technique the CO2 Emissions project
  uses for week-of-year.
- **`duration_min`** — `duration_ms / 60000`, a pure readability
  transform.
- **`mood_quadrant`** — buckets each track into one of four moods
  (energetic/calm x happy/dark) from Russell's circumplex model of
  affect, using training-data medians of `valence`/`energy` as the
  quadrant boundaries. A classifier can already learn this distinction
  from the raw floats; this feature exists for human legibility in the
  notebook and app.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based.features import FeatureEngineer

sample = tracks_df.sample(3000, random_state=config.RANDOM_SEED)
engineered = FeatureEngineer().fit_transform(sample)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
sns.scatterplot(data=engineered, x="valence", y="energy", hue="mood_quadrant", alpha=0.5, ax=ax, palette=PALETTE[:4])
ax.set_title("Every sampled track's (valence, energy), colored by mood_quadrant")
plt.show()
```

## Methodology

### The recommender: weighted nearest-neighbor search

`ContentRecommender` (`content_based/model.py`) standardizes every audio
feature (scale matters directly for distance, unlike a tree-based
model), then finds the `k` nearest tracks by Euclidean distance in that
feature space. Three optional ways to reshape that distance metric
before the search runs, each evaluated below rather than assumed to
help:

- **Importance-weighted** — fit a genre classifier on the same features
  and use its learned feature importances to *weight* the distance
  metric.
- **PCA** — project onto the top 10 principal components before
  searching. With only ~25 features to begin with, this is more a test
  of whether discarding lower-variance components denoises the space
  than a dimensionality-curse fix.
- **NCA** (Neighborhood Components Analysis) — learn a linear projection
  via gradient descent that directly maximizes KNN accuracy under the
  genre labels. Its cost scales roughly quadratically with row count and
  gets OOM-killed on this project's full ~72k-row training split
  (verified directly), so it's fit on a 5,000-row subsample instead.

### Evaluating a recommender with no user-feedback data: precision@k

There's no click-through or replay data here, so this project uses
**precision@k**: hold out a set of tracks, recommend `k` tracks for each
from the remaining catalog, and measure what fraction of those
recommendations share the query track's true genre — a rough proxy for
"actually sounds alike," the standard fallback when no real feedback
signal exists.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based import model

train_df, test_df = model.train_test_split_tracks(tracks_df, test_size=0.2)

X_train, y_train = data.split_features_target(train_df)
classifier_pipeline = model.build_classifier_pipeline(model.random_forest_estimator())
classifier_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
weights = model.compute_feature_weights_from_classifier(classifier_pipeline)

results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"approach": "Popularity baseline", "precision_at_10": model.popularity_baseline_precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10)},
    {"approach": "Unweighted KNN", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10)},
    {"approach": "Importance-weighted KNN", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, feature_weights=weights)},
    {"approach": "PCA(10) KNN", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, embedding=model.pca_embedding(10))},
    {
        "approach": "NCA(10) KNN",
        "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(
            train_df, test_df, k=10, embedding=model.nca_embedding(10), embedding_fit_sample_size=5000
        ),
    },
])
results
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.barh(results["approach"], results["precision_at_10"], color=[PALETTE[3], PALETTE[2], PALETTE[0], PALETTE[1], PALETTE[4]])
ax.set_xlabel("Precision@10")
plt.show()
```

Importance-weighted KNN was the best of the five — the more
"principled" methods (PCA, NCA) didn't beat this simpler heuristic here,
a result only knowable by measuring, not by assuming a fancier-sounding
technique wins.

### Is exact-genre matching too strict?

Several of this dataset's 113 genre tags are near-synonyms applied to
the *same physical track* — verified directly: 24,259 of the raw
114,000 rows are exact-duplicate `track_id`s carrying a different genre
tag each time. `genre_families.py` groups the 113 tags into 13 broader
families (plus a `mood_context` bucket for tags like `chill`/`sad`/
`study` that are playlist moods, not musical genres) to see how much of
that gap is near-synonym mismatches.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based.genre_families import GENRE_TO_FAMILY

granularity = pd.DataFrame([
    {"approach": "Popularity baseline", "granularity": "Exact genre", "precision_at_10": model.popularity_baseline_precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10)},
    {"approach": "Popularity baseline", "granularity": "Genre family", "precision_at_10": model.popularity_baseline_precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, genre_map=GENRE_TO_FAMILY)},
    {"approach": "Importance-weighted KNN", "granularity": "Exact genre", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, feature_weights=weights)},
    {"approach": "Importance-weighted KNN", "granularity": "Genre family", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, feature_weights=weights, genre_map=GENRE_TO_FAMILY)},
])
granularity.pivot(index="approach", columns="granularity", values="precision_at_10")
```

The popularity baseline jumps ~14x at the looser genre-family
granularity, while the recommender only roughly doubles — so the
recommender's advantage over the naive baseline is actually *larger* in
relative terms at the strict exact-genre level (~18x) than at the
family level (~2.7x). Coarser bins flatter every method's absolute
score, including guessing.

## Interpretability: what separates genres?

The genre classifier exists specifically to produce the importance
weights above and to be explained — not to be a high-scoring classifier
in its own right (114 genres is a genuinely hard multiclass problem).

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based.interpretability import compute_shap_values, top_shap_features

explanation, _ = compute_shap_values(classifier_pipeline, X_train, max_samples=500)
top = top_shap_features(explanation, top_n=10).sort_values("mean_abs_shap")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5))
ax.barh(top["feature"], top["mean_abs_shap"], color=PALETTE[0])
ax.set_xlabel("Mean |SHAP value|")
ax.set_title("Top 10 features distinguishing genres")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Captured for the head-to-head comparison later in this report.
cb_best_precision_exact = results.set_index("approach").loc["Importance-weighted KNN", "precision_at_10"]
cb_best_precision_family = granularity.set_index(["approach", "granularity"]).loc[
    ("Importance-weighted KNN", "Genre family"), "precision_at_10"
]
cb_baseline_precision = results.set_index("approach").loc["Popularity baseline", "precision_at_10"]
```

# Part II — Collaborative Filtering (KKBox)

Given a real member's listening history and a specific song, predict
whether they'll listen to it again within a month of first hearing it —
built on Kaggle's real [WSDM — KKBox's Music Recommendation
Challenge](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kkbox-music-recommendation-challenge)
(2018). Unlike Part I, this needs no audio content at all — the whole
task is defined by real user/song interaction history, and there's a
real Kaggle leaderboard here, scored by AUC.

## Data

Four tables, verified directly against the real downloaded files:

- **`train.csv`/`test.csv`** (7,377,418 / 2,556,791 rows): one row per
  listening event — `msno` (member), `song_id`, three context columns
  (`source_system_tab`, `source_screen_name`, `source_type`), and
  (train only) `target`.
- **`songs.csv`** (2,296,834 rows): `song_length`, `genre_ids`,
  `artist_name`, `composer`, `lyricist`, `language`.
- **`members.csv`** (34,403 rows): `city`, `bd` (self-reported age),
  `gender`, `registered_via`, `registration_init_time`, `expiration_date`.
- **`song_extra_info.csv`** (2,296,870 rows): `name`, `isrc`.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.collaborative import config, data

train_sample = data.load_train().sample(50_000, random_state=config.RANDOM_SEED)
panel_sample = data.merge_side_tables(train_sample)
print(f"target balance (sample): {panel_sample[config.TARGET_COL].mean():.3f}")
panel_sample.describe(include="all").T.head(10)
```

Verified directly on the full 7.4M-row `train.csv`: `target` is close to
balanced (50.4% replay / 49.6% no-replay) — unlike academic_success's
imbalanced classes, no resampling (ADASYN etc.) is needed here.

### Real data-quality issues, found by checking rather than assuming

- **`bd` (age) is garbage for ~58% of members** — 0 (the unset default),
  negative values, and a maximum of **1051**. Anything outside 5-100
  becomes `NaN` rather than a trusted age.
- **`gender` missing for ~58%**, **`composer` missing for ~47%**,
  **`lyricist` missing for ~85%** — all three are used only as coarse
  presence signals, not rich per-value features.
- **`genre_ids` is multi-valued for ~7.9%** of songs (pipe-separated) —
  counted, not just checked for presence.
- **`artist_name` has 222,363 distinct values** — far too many to
  one-hot encode; replaced with a frequency encoding instead (see
  Methodology).

## Feature engineering

`src/recommendation_showcase/collaborative/features.py` is the single
source of truth for turning these raw, messy columns into model-ready
features:

- **`InteractionCountEncoder`**: learns `song_popularity`,
  `user_activity_count`, and `artist_song_count` from the *training*
  interactions only (a song/user/artist never seen in training gets 0 —
  itself meaningful signal, not a gap to fill). This is the
  collaborative-filtering analogue of Part I's evaluation discipline:
  learn a lookup from training data only, apply it unchanged to any
  future row.
- **`FeatureEngineer`**: `member_tenure_days` (registration to
  expiration), `age_clean` (the garbage-`bd` fix above), `genre_count`/
  `primary_genre` (from pipe-separated `genre_ids`), `composer_count`/
  `has_composer`/`has_lyricist`, and `isrc_country`/`isrc_year` (parsed
  from `song_extra_info.isrc`, with a century pivot for the 2-digit year).
- **`RareCategoryGrouper`**: the same technique academic_success uses,
  applied here to `primary_genre` (182 distinct values) rather than
  occupation/nationality codes.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.collaborative.features import FeatureEngineer, InteractionCountEncoder

X_sample = panel_sample.drop(columns=[config.TARGET_COL])
counted = InteractionCountEncoder().fit_transform(X_sample)
engineered = FeatureEngineer().fit_transform(counted)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
sns.histplot(engineered["age_clean"].dropna(), bins=40, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("age_clean (garbage removed)")
sns.histplot(counted["song_popularity"], bins=50, ax=axes[1], log_scale=(False, True))
axes[1].set_title("song_popularity (log y)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Methodology

### Why one train/holdout split, not k-fold cross-validation

At 7.4M rows, a single fit of a gradient-boosted model already takes
real time (verified directly: LightGBM, ~91 seconds for the full join +
feature engineering + fit). Unlike Part I, there's no chronological or
identity-based leakage risk here that would make a single stratified
split misleading — so one honest 80/20 split, not 5-fold CV, is the
tractable and still-honest choice.

### Model comparison

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.collaborative import model

sweep_sample = data.load_train().sample(300_000, random_state=config.RANDOM_SEED)
sweep_panel = data.merge_side_tables(sweep_sample)

sweep_results = []
for name, factory in model.MODEL_FACTORIES.items():
    result = model.holdout_eval(sweep_panel, estimator=factory())
    sweep_results.append({"model": name, "auc": result["auc"]})
sweep_df = pd.DataFrame(sweep_results).sort_values("auc", ascending=False)
sweep_df
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.barh(sweep_df["model"], sweep_df["auc"], color=PALETTE[0])
ax.set_xlabel("AUC (300k-row sample)")
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.show()
```

Random Forest is excluded from `scripts/train_collaborative.py`'s
default by design — verified directly that
`RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=12)` didn't finish
fitting on the full 5.9M-row training split even after 500 seconds,
while LightGBM finished the equivalent job in 91 seconds. The sweep
above uses a 300k-row sample specifically so Random Forest *can* be
included for a fair comparison point — not because it would scale to
the real dataset.

### Full-scale result

```{python}
full_panel = data.load_full_train_panel()
full_result = model.holdout_eval(full_panel, estimator=model.default_estimator())
print(f"LightGBM, full 7.4M-row panel: AUC = {full_result['auc']:.4f}")
print(f"  (trained on {full_result['n_train']:,} rows, evaluated on {full_result['n_holdout']:,})")
```

# Head-to-Head Comparison

Both approaches solve "recommend a song," but they aren't
interchangeable — the honest comparison is about what each technique
needs and what it's actually good for, not which number is bigger.

```{python}
comparison = pd.DataFrame([
    {
        "Aspect": "Data required",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "None — just item features",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "Real user/item interaction history",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Cold-start (brand-new item/user)",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "New tracks work immediately (their own features exist)",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "New songs/users get 0 interaction counts — a real weakness",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Evaluation metric",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "precision@k (genre-sharing proxy)",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "AUC (real Kaggle leaderboard)",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Headline result",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": f"{cb_best_precision_exact:.3f} precision@10 (exact genre), {cb_best_precision_family:.3f} (genre family) — vs. {cb_baseline_precision:.3f} popularity baseline",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": f"{coll_auc:.4f} AUC, full 7.4M-row training set",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Explains recommendations by",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "Feature similarity (radar chart of audio properties)",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "Interaction frequency + member/song attributes (SHAP)",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Dataset scale",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "~90k tracks (deduplicated)",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "7.4M interactions, 2.3M songs, 34k members",
    },
])
comparison
```

Neither number in the "Headline result" row is comparable to the other
in any direct sense — precision@10 and AUC measure different things on
different tasks. What *is* comparable is the discipline behind each: both
projects hold out data honestly, compare against a naive baseline before
claiming a win, and measure scalability/cost tradeoffs directly rather
than assuming them (NCA's memory limit in Part I; Random Forest's
full-scale timeout in Part II).

# Discussion

- **Part I's importance-weighted KNN won** its own comparison, beating
  unweighted KNN, PCA, and NCA — the two more mathematically
  sophisticated methods didn't pay off here. This is a genuine,
  reportable finding in the same spirit as the CO2 Emissions and
  academic_success projects' own honestly-reported negative results
  (ADASYN, stacking).
- **Part I's exact-genre precision@k understates recommendation
  quality, but not by as much as it might look** — the naive baseline's
  score grows even faster at the looser genre-family granularity, so
  the recommender's real edge is clearest at the strict, exact-genre
  level.
- **Part II's real, measured scalability finding**: Random Forest
  doesn't finish fitting on the full KKBox training set in a reasonable
  time, while LightGBM does the same job in under two minutes — worth
  knowing before assuming a bigger, ostensibly-more-powerful ensemble
  is always the safer default.
- A limitation worth naming for both: Part I's genre-sharing is an
  imperfect proxy for "sounds alike"; Part II's single train/holdout
  split (not k-fold CV) is an honest tradeoff for training cost, but one
  fold's variance is real.

# Conclusion

Content-based and collaborative filtering solve the same stated problem
— "recommend something" — with almost entirely non-overlapping
requirements, evaluation strategies, and failure modes. Building both on
real data, under the same standards of honest evaluation and measured
(not assumed) engineering tradeoffs, makes the actual difference between
the two techniques legible in a way that reading about either one in the
abstract doesn't.
